title: Gastrointestinal physiology — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Physiology Digestive System lecture + syllabus

questions.stem: The two smooth-muscle layers of the muscularis externa are separated by the
questions.why: The myenteric plexus occupies the plane between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa. Its enteric neurons coordinate gastrointestinal muscle activity, including propulsive contractions and relaxation.

notes.B: The submucosal plexus lies in the submucosa and chiefly regulates mucosal secretion and local blood flow, rather than separating the external muscle layers.
notes.C: The lamina propria is connective tissue beneath the mucosal epithelium, containing vessels, immune cells and glands, rather than lying between the external muscle layers.
notes.D: The muscularis mucosae is a thin smooth-muscle layer separating the mucosa from the submucosa and producing local mucosal movements.
notes.E: The serosa forms the outer covering of intraperitoneal gut segments and lies external to the muscularis externa, not between its layers.

questions.stem: The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus is mainly responsible for controlling
questions.why: The submucosal plexus integrates local sensory information and regulates epithelial secretion, absorption, mucosal blood flow and muscularis mucosae activity. The myenteric plexus is more directly associated with coordinating contractions of the muscularis externa.

notes.A: The migrating motor complex involves coordinated gastrointestinal motility and fasting signals such as motilin, rather than being chiefly a submucosal secretory function.
notes.C: The force and propagation of peristaltic contractions are primarily coordinated by myenteric circuits acting on the muscularis externa.
notes.D: Pharyngeal swallowing is coordinated by brainstem circuits and cranial motor nerves rather than the intrinsic submucosal enteric plexus.
notes.E: Gastric emptying depends on antral motility, pyloric resistance and duodenal feedback, rather than being the principal function of the submucosal plexus.

questions.stem: The submucosal plexus is notably absent from the
questions.why: Submucosal ganglia form plexuses in the small and large intestine but not in the stomach or oesophagus.

questions.stem: The lymphoid tissue that defends the gut against luminal bacteria lies chiefly in the
questions.why: Gut-associated lymphoid tissue includes diffuse lymphocytes, plasma cells and organised lymphoid follicles within the mucosa, particularly the lamina propria. Larger aggregates may extend into the submucosa, enabling immune surveillance and protection against luminal antigens.

notes.A: The serosa provides an external mesothelial covering and connective tissue but is not the principal compartment for immune surveillance immediately beneath the mucosal epithelium.
notes.B: The submucosal plexus is a network of enteric neurons controlling local mucosal functions, not a collection of lymphoid immune cells.
notes.C: The muscularis mucosae consists chiefly of smooth muscle that produces local mucosal movements, rather than housing most mucosal lymphoid cells.
notes.E: The muscularis externa generates major mixing and propulsive movements and is not the principal location of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: GI smooth muscle behaves as a functional syncytium because its fibres are joined by
questions.why: Gap junctions connect neighbouring gastrointestinal smooth-muscle cells through low-resistance channels that permit ionic current to spread between cells. This electrical coupling allows groups of cells to depolarise and contract together as a functional syncytium.

notes.A: Desmosomes provide mechanical adhesion and resistance to tissue stress but do not themselves provide the intercellular ionic channels needed for electrical coupling.
notes.B: Tight junctions restrict paracellular movement between epithelial cells and maintain barrier properties, rather than allowing electrical current to pass directly between smooth-muscle cells.
notes.C: Chemical synapses transmit signals using neurotransmitters, but direct electrical coupling between adjacent smooth-muscle cells is principally mediated by gap junctions.
notes.D: A basement membrane supports cells and helps organise extracellular structure but does not create low-resistance cytoplasmic channels between neighbouring smooth-muscle fibres.

questions.stem: The pacemaker cells that generate the slow waves (basic electrical rhythm) of the gut are the
questions.why: Interstitial cells of Cajal generate rhythmic oscillations in membrane potential and transmit them to electrically coupled gastrointestinal smooth muscle. These slow waves establish the timing of phasic contractions, with contraction strength influenced by neural and hormonal inputs.

notes.B: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor in gastric glands, rather than generating the electrical rhythms of gastrointestinal muscle.
notes.C: Enterochromaffin-like cells release histamine to stimulate gastric acid secretion and are not the specialised gastrointestinal electrical pacemaker cells.
notes.D: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages of hepatic sinusoids and participate in phagocytosis and immune surveillance rather than intestinal electrical pacing.
notes.E: Paneth cells at the base of intestinal crypts secrete antimicrobial substances, including defensins, and do not generate smooth-muscle slow waves.

questions.stem: Slow waves themselves do not cause contraction unless they reach threshold and trigger
questions.why: Slow waves bring the membrane toward threshold; the superimposed spike potentials actually drive contraction.

questions.stem: Noradrenaline and adrenaline affect gut smooth muscle by causing
questions.why: Sympathetic catecholaminergic signalling generally inhibits gastrointestinal wall motility through suppression of excitatory enteric transmission and, in many preparations, smooth-muscle hyperpolarisation or relaxation. Responses vary with receptor subtype and region; sphincters may instead contract.

notes.A: Slow-wave frequency is primarily established by interstitial cells of Cajal and varies by gastrointestinal region, rather than necessarily increasing with sympathetic stimulation.
notes.B: Tonic contraction can occur in gastrointestinal sphincters during sympathetic activity, but the general response of the non-sphincter muscle wall is reduced motility.
notes.D: Depolarisation towards threshold tends to increase excitability and contractile activity, whereas sympathetic input generally suppresses excitatory activity in the gastrointestinal wall.
notes.E: Sympathetic postganglionic fibres supplying most gastrointestinal targets release noradrenaline and can inhibit acetylcholine release from excitatory enteric neurons.

questions.stem: A tonic (sustained) contraction, rather than a phasic one, is characteristic of the
questions.why: The lower oesophageal sphincter maintains a sustained basal smooth-muscle contraction that creates a high-pressure zone and limits gastro-oesophageal reflux. It relaxes transiently during swallowing, allowing the bolus to enter the stomach.

notes.A: Small-intestinal wall muscle commonly produces rhythmic phasic segmentation and peristalsis for mixing and propulsion, rather than maintaining a continuously closed sphincter.
notes.B: The oesophageal body generates sequential propulsive contractions during swallowing, whereas sustained basal barrier pressure characterises its sphincter regions.
notes.C: The transverse colon exhibits mixing and propagating contractile patterns, rather than functioning as a continuously contracted gastro-oesophageal barrier.
notes.E: The gastric antrum produces strong phasic contractions that grind and propel gastric contents, contrasting with the sustained basal tone of the lower oesophageal sphincter.

questions.stem: The migrating motor complex that sweeps undigested residue along the gut between meals recurs about every
questions.why: During fasting, the migrating motor complex recurs approximately every 90–120 minutes, with a phase of strong propagating contractions that clears residual material. Feeding interrupts the fasting pattern and replaces it with fed-state motility.

notes.A: Ten to fifteen minutes is much shorter than the usual interval between successive migrating motor complexes in the fasting gastrointestinal tract.
notes.B: Six to eight hours substantially exceeds the typical 90–120-minute fasting cycle and would omit several expected migrating motor complexes.
notes.C: Thirty seconds is closer to the timescale of individual contractile events than the interval between complete fasting motor complexes.
notes.D: Twelve hours spans numerous normal fasting motor cycles, rather than representing the recurrence interval of a single migrating motor complex.

questions.stem: The hormone that initiates the migrating motor complex is
questions.why: Motilin is released cyclically by endocrine cells of the upper small intestine during fasting and is closely associated with gastric phase III migrating motor complex activity. Enteric and other regulatory mechanisms also contribute, especially to intestinal-origin complexes.

notes.B: Secretin is released in response to acidic duodenal contents and chiefly promotes bicarbonate secretion, rather than initiating the characteristic fasting motor pattern.
notes.C: Cholecystokinin is released after nutrients enter the small intestine and promotes pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction, rather than driving the fasting complex.
notes.D: Gastrin promotes gastric acid secretion and influences gastric motility, but is not the characteristic cyclical hormone associated with fasting phase III activity.
notes.E: Somatostatin generally inhibits gastrointestinal hormone release and several secretory functions, rather than serving as the principal hormonal trigger of gastric fasting phase III.

questions.stem: Segmentation contractions differ from peristalsis in that they mainly

options.label: B
options.text: mix chyme with secretions rather than propel it

options.label: C
options.text: propel chyme rapidly toward the anus

options.label: E
options.text: are driven by the pharyngeal constrictors

questions.why: Segmentation consists of alternating local contractions of circular smooth muscle that divide and redistribute chyme. This increases contact with digestive secretions and the absorptive epithelium, whereas peristaltic waves primarily move contents along the tract.

notes.A: Emptying solid food from the stomach requires antral grinding and coordinated pyloric opening; this is not the defining purpose of intestinal segmentation.
notes.C: Rapid net propulsion towards the anus characterises propulsive motor patterns, whereas segmentation chiefly produces local redistribution and mixing of luminal contents.
notes.D: Segmentation is especially important in the small intestine and is not confined to the oesophagus, whose major motor function is bolus propulsion.
notes.E: Pharyngeal constrictors propel a swallowed bolus through the pharynx using skeletal muscle, rather than producing intestinal smooth-muscle segmentation.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic supply to the distal colon and anorectal region is carried by the
questions.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from sacral spinal segments S2–S4 and carry parasympathetic preganglionic fibres to the distal colon and rectum. They support distal bowel motility and contribute to the defaecation reflex.

notes.A: Hypogastric nerves predominantly convey sympathetic pathways to pelvic organs and do not provide the principal sacral parasympathetic input to the distal bowel.
notes.B: The phrenic nerve arises mainly from cervical spinal segments C3–C5 and supplies the diaphragm rather than parasympathetic gastrointestinal motor pathways.
notes.D: The vagus provides parasympathetic innervation to the foregut and midgut, whereas the distal hindgut receives sacral parasympathetic fibres.
notes.E: Thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves generally carry sympathetic fibres; the specifically named pelvic splanchnic nerves provide the sacral parasympathetic supply.

questions.stem: Sympathetic preganglionic fibres to the gut arise from spinal segments
questions.why: Gastrointestinal sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from thoracic and upper lumbar spinal segments, approximately T5–L2. Their axons commonly travel in splanchnic nerves and synapse in prevertebral ganglia before postganglionic fibres reach the gut.

notes.A: Upper cervical spinal segments contain motor and sensory pathways but do not form the principal thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow supplying abdominal digestive organs.
notes.B: Upper thoracic sympathetic segments chiefly contribute to pathways serving thoracic and upper-body structures; the major gastrointestinal outflow begins further caudally.
notes.C: Lower lumbar segments L3–L5 are below the conventional T1–L2 sympathetic preganglionic outflow and do not supply its principal gastrointestinal component.
notes.E: Sacral segments S2–S4 provide pelvic parasympathetic outflow to the distal bowel, rather than the thoracolumbar sympathetic preganglionic supply.

questions.stem: In general, sympathetic stimulation of the gastrointestinal tract causes

options.label: A
options.text: increased motility and secretion with sphincter relaxation

options.label: B
options.text: copious watery secretion from all glands

options.label: D
options.text: release of gastrin from G cells

options.label: E
options.text: inhibition of motility and secretion with sphincter contraction

questions.why: Sympathetic input generally inhibits gastrointestinal secretion and wall motility by suppressing excitatory enteric transmission and altering smooth-muscle activity. It can increase sphincter tone and constrict splanchnic vessels, particularly during stress.

notes.A: Enhanced digestive motility and secretion with coordinated sphincter relaxation are generally associated with parasympathetic and excitatory enteric activity, rather than sympathetic predominance.
notes.B: Copious watery glandular secretion is characteristic of selected parasympathetic secretory responses, not a uniform effect of sympathetic stimulation throughout the gastrointestinal tract.
notes.C: The detrusor is urinary bladder smooth muscle, and its contraction is mainly mediated by parasympathetic pathways rather than representing a gastrointestinal sympathetic response.
notes.D: Gastrin release is principally promoted by luminal peptides, gastric distension and vagal gastrin-releasing peptide signalling, not the general inhibitory gastrointestinal sympathetic response.

questions.stem: Of the roughly 9 litres of fluid passing through the GI tract each day, the amount actually ingested is only about
questions.why: Approximately two litres of fluid are ingested daily, with a further seven litres contributed by saliva and gastrointestinal, pancreatic and biliary secretions. Most of this combined luminal fluid is reabsorbed before faecal excretion.

notes.B: Seven litres approximates the daily contribution of endogenous digestive secretions in this teaching model, rather than the amount consumed directly.
notes.C: Nine litres approximates the total fluid load entering the digestive tract after combining oral intake with endogenous secretions.
notes.D: Half a litre is lower than the approximate daily oral fluid contribution used in this conventional gastrointestinal fluid-balance calculation.
notes.E: Five litres exceeds the conventional two-litre oral intake estimate and does not represent the standard partition of the nine-litre luminal load.

questions.stem: Salivary amylase is produced by which type of acinar cell?
questions.why: Serous acinar cells synthesise and package digestive proteins, including salivary alpha-amylase, into apical secretory granules. Amylase initiates starch digestion by hydrolysing internal alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, while mucous acinar cells principally produce mucins.

notes.A: Paneth cells are intestinal crypt cells that secrete antimicrobial proteins such as lysozyme and defensins, rather than producing salivary amylase.
notes.C: Mucous acinar cells principally secrete mucins that lubricate oral contents, whereas enzyme-rich watery secretion is characteristic of serous acinar cells.
notes.D: Salivary duct cells primarily modify the electrolyte composition of acinar secretion, rather than serving as the principal site of salivary amylase synthesis.
notes.E: Goblet cells are unicellular mucus-secreting epithelial glands and are not the enzyme-producing serous acinar cells of major salivary glands.

questions.stem: The final saliva reaching the mouth is hypotonic because the duct cells

options.label: A
options.text: are freely permeable to water throughout

options.label: C
options.text: reabsorb more Na+ than the K+ they secrete

options.label: D
options.text: secrete Na+ and reabsorb K+ freely with water

options.label: E
options.text: add large amounts of NaCl to the primary secretion

questions.why: Salivary ducts reabsorb sodium and chloride while secreting potassium and bicarbonate. Because net solute removal occurs across a relatively water-impermeable ductal epithelium, final saliva becomes hypotonic, especially at lower flow rates.

notes.A: High ductal water permeability would allow water to follow reabsorbed solutes, reducing the osmotic separation needed to produce markedly hypotonic saliva.
notes.B: Salivary duct cells generally secrete bicarbonate into the lumen; bicarbonate reabsorption is not the principal mechanism underlying final salivary hypotonicity.
notes.D: The usual net ductal transport involves sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion, rather than sodium secretion with free water movement and potassium uptake.
notes.E: Adding substantial sodium chloride would increase luminal solute concentration; salivary hypotonicity instead depends on net ductal electrolyte removal without equivalent water reabsorption.

questions.stem: Unusually among digestive secretions, salivation is controlled

options.label: C
options.text: only by the parasympathetic system, sympathetic having no effect

options.label: D
options.text: purely by neural reflexes, with both ANS branches increasing it

questions.why: Salivary secretion is regulated predominantly by autonomic neural reflexes rather than by the major gastrointestinal secretory hormones. Both parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves can stimulate secretion, with different effects on fluid volume and protein composition.

notes.A: Sympathetic stimulation can evoke protein-rich secretion, but parasympathetic activity is also important and typically produces abundant salivary fluid.
notes.B: Secretin is a duodenal hormone that stimulates pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate-rich secretion, rather than acting as the principal regulator of salivation.
notes.C: Parasympathetic activity strongly stimulates salivation, but sympathetic nerves also stimulate salivary protein secretion and cannot be considered physiologically inactive.
notes.E: Gastrin principally stimulates gastric acid secretion and is not the main control signal for the neural reflex regulation of salivary glands.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands evokes saliva that is

options.label: B
options.text: rich in digestive enzymes but low in water

options.label: E
options.text: copious and watery, relatively poor in protein

questions.why: Parasympathetic cholinergic stimulation activates muscarinic receptors and promotes substantial fluid and electrolyte secretion from salivary acini, supported by increased glandular perfusion. The resulting saliva is generally copious and relatively dilute in protein compared with sympathetic secretion.

notes.A: Relatively scant, protein-rich saliva is more characteristic of sympathetic stimulation, although actual secretion composition also depends on gland type and stimulus intensity.
notes.B: Enzyme secretion may accompany parasympathetic activation, but abundant water secretion is a defining feature rather than a low fluid output.
notes.C: Parasympathetic saliva contains electrolytes and gland-specific proteins, and it is not inherently acidic or devoid of digestive enzymes.
notes.D: Both autonomic divisions stimulate salivary glands, but they differ in their relative effects on fluid secretion, protein release and vascular responses.

questions.stem: The parotid gland receives its parasympathetic secretomotor supply from the

options.label: A
options.text: glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion

options.label: B
options.text: facial nerve via the submandibular ganglion

options.label: C
options.text: vagus nerve via the nodose ganglion

options.label: D
options.text: trigeminal nerve via the ciliary ganglion

questions.why: Parotid preganglionic parasympathetic fibres originate from the glossopharyngeal nerve and travel through the tympanic and lesser petrosal pathways to the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibres reach the gland through the auriculotemporal nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve.

notes.B: Facial nerve fibres travel through the chorda tympani to the submandibular ganglion, supplying mainly the submandibular and sublingual glands rather than the parotid.
notes.C: The nodose ganglion is a sensory ganglion of the vagus nerve, not the parasympathetic relay for parotid secretomotor fibres.
notes.D: The ciliary ganglion relays oculomotor parasympathetic fibres to intraocular muscles; trigeminal branches carry hitchhiking fibres but do not originate parotid parasympathetic outflow.
notes.E: The hypoglossal nerve primarily supplies tongue muscles and does not directly provide the preganglionic secretomotor pathway to the parotid gland.

questions.stem: The pharyngeal phase of swallowing is

options.label: A
options.text: entirely controlled by the enteric nervous system

options.label: B
options.text: involuntary and lasts about one second

options.label: D
options.text: voluntary and under cortical control throughout

options.label: E
options.text: involuntary and lasts about ten seconds

questions.why: Once the bolus reaches the pharynx, sensory input triggers a coordinated, largely involuntary brainstem swallowing sequence. The pharyngeal phase is rapid, typically around one second, and briefly protects the airway while directing food into the oesophagus.

notes.A: The enteric nervous system coordinates many oesophageal and intestinal functions, but pharyngeal swallowing requires brainstem control of striated muscle through cranial nerves.
notes.C: Voluntary control primarily initiates the oral phase, whereas the subsequent rapid pharyngeal sequence is largely reflexly coordinated.
notes.D: The cerebral cortex can initiate and modulate swallowing, but the pharyngeal motor sequence is not maintained entirely by voluntary cortical control.
notes.E: A duration of around ten seconds better approximates some oesophageal transit times than the brief, coordinated pharyngeal phase of swallowing.

questions.stem: During the pharyngeal phase of swallowing, entry of food into the nasopharynx is prevented by

options.label: A
options.text: relaxation of the upper oesophageal sphincter

options.label: B
options.text: elevation of the tongue against the hard palate

options.label: D
options.text: closure of the lower oesophageal sphincter

questions.why: Elevation and posterior movement of the soft palate close the velopharyngeal opening during swallowing. This separates the nasopharynx from the oropharynx, directing the bolus towards the oesophagus and limiting nasal regurgitation.

notes.A: Upper oesophageal sphincter relaxation opens the passage into the oesophagus, but it does not directly close the route into the nasopharynx.
notes.B: Tongue elevation helps propel the bolus backwards during the oral phase, whereas nasopharyngeal closure requires movement of the soft palate.
notes.D: Lower oesophageal sphincter closure helps prevent gastric reflux and occurs far below the velopharyngeal opening that must be sealed during pharyngeal swallowing.
notes.E: The diaphragm contributes to respiratory and lower oesophageal mechanics, rather than directly sealing the nasopharynx during the pharyngeal swallowing sequence.

questions.stem: Secondary peristaltic waves in the oesophagus are triggered by

options.label: A
options.text: relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: local oesophageal distension via the enteric nervous system

options.label: E
options.text: the swallowing centre at the start of each swallow

questions.why: Secondary oesophageal peristalsis is triggered by residual food or distension within the oesophagus rather than a new voluntary swallow. Local enteric mechanosensory circuits and vagal pathways coordinate a clearing wave, with their relative contributions depending on oesophageal region.

notes.A: Lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation permits bolus entry into the stomach but is not the usual initiating stimulus for a secondary clearing contraction.
notes.B: Stimulation of pharyngeal receptors helps initiate the swallowing sequence and primary peristalsis, whereas secondary waves respond to oesophageal distension.
notes.C: Diaphragmatic contraction contributes to pressure around the gastro-oesophageal junction but does not normally initiate secondary peristaltic clearance of retained material.
notes.E: The swallowing centre initiates primary oesophageal peristalsis during a swallow; secondary peristalsis can begin without a new pharyngeal swallowing event.

questions.stem: The swallowing (deglutition) centre is located in the
questions.why: Swallowing is coordinated by a brainstem central pattern-generating network centred in the medulla, with contributions from adjacent pontine circuitry. Sensory input and coordinated cranial motor output organise pharyngeal propulsion, airway protection and oesophageal entry.

notes.A: The cerebral cortex participates in voluntary swallow initiation and modulation, but the core patterned pharyngeal swallowing sequence is organised within brainstem circuits.
notes.B: The hypothalamus regulates appetite, thirst and autonomic homeostasis, but it is not the principal neural centre coordinating the rapid swallowing motor sequence.
notes.C: The cerebellum contributes to motor coordination and timing, whereas the core swallowing pattern generator is located in the brainstem.
notes.D: The spinal cord contains motor and autonomic pathways but does not house the principal cranial nerve circuits coordinating pharyngeal swallowing.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor are both secreted by the gastric
questions.why: Gastric parietal cells in oxyntic glands secrete hydrochloric acid through apical proton pumps and intrinsic factor as a glycoprotein. Acid supports digestion and antimicrobial defence, while intrinsic factor enables efficient vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

notes.B: Chief cells primarily release pepsinogen and gastric lipase, rather than secreting the acid and intrinsic factor characteristic of parietal cells.
notes.C: G cells secrete gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion indirectly and directly through gastric regulatory pathways, but do not themselves produce hydrochloric acid.
notes.D: Mucous neck cells produce mucus within gastric glands, supporting lubrication and protection rather than supplying intrinsic factor and hydrochloric acid.
notes.E: Enterochromaffin-like cells secrete histamine, which activates parietal-cell H2 receptors, but the acid and intrinsic factor originate from parietal cells themselves.

questions.stem: Pepsinogen and gastric lipase are products of the gastric
questions.why: Gastric chief cells synthesise and secrete pepsinogen, an inactive precursor converted to pepsin in the acidic gastric lumen, and gastric lipase. These secretions initiate protein and lipid digestion before chyme enters the small intestine.

notes.A: Surface mucous cells secrete protective mucus and bicarbonate, forming a barrier against gastric acid and pepsin rather than supplying the principal gastric digestive enzymes.
notes.C: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor; their acid activates pepsinogen but does not originate from the enzyme-producing chief-cell pathway.
notes.D: G cells release gastrin into the circulation to regulate gastric secretion and motility, rather than secreting pepsinogen or gastric lipase into the lumen.
notes.E: D cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits gastrin and other secretory pathways, rather than producing the digestive enzyme products of chief cells.

questions.stem: In the parietal cell, H+ is secreted into the lumen in exchange for K+ by the
questions.why: The apical hydrogen–potassium ATPase uses ATP to exchange intracellular hydrogen ions for luminal potassium ions across the parietal-cell canalicular membrane. Chloride enters the lumen separately, allowing hydrochloric acid to accumulate in gastric juice.

notes.A: The basolateral chloride–bicarbonate exchanger supplies intracellular chloride and transfers bicarbonate to blood, but does not directly pump hydrogen ions into the gastric lumen.
notes.B: The sodium–potassium–chloride cotransporter mediates coupled electrolyte movement in several epithelia, rather than performing the ATP-driven apical hydrogen–potassium exchange of gastric acid secretion.
notes.D: The sodium–potassium ATPase maintains cellular sodium and potassium gradients, chiefly at the basolateral membrane, rather than directly secreting gastric hydrogen ions.
notes.E: Sodium–hydrogen exchange contributes to intracellular pH regulation in many cells but is not the principal apical proton pump responsible for gastric acid secretion.

questions.stem: The slight rise in venous blood pH after a meal, caused by bicarbonate leaving the parietal cell, is called the
questions.why: During gastric acid secretion, carbonic anhydrase generates hydrogen ions and bicarbonate from carbon dioxide and water. Bicarbonate exits parietal cells basolaterally in exchange for chloride, temporarily increasing gastric venous blood alkalinity after a meal.

notes.A: The Bohr effect describes reduced haemoglobin oxygen affinity with increased carbon dioxide or hydrogen ion concentration, rather than postprandial bicarbonate entry into venous blood.
notes.B: An acid tide would imply increased acidity, whereas secretion of gastric hydrogen ions is accompanied by bicarbonate transfer into the blood.
notes.C: Alkaline reflux refers to reflux of relatively alkaline gastrointestinal contents and does not describe the transient rise in venous alkalinity accompanying gastric acid secretion.
notes.E: The chloride shift usually describes chloride–bicarbonate exchange in erythrocytes during carbon dioxide transport; the postprandial venous change is specifically termed the alkaline tide.

questions.stem: Intrinsic factor is essential because it is required for the absorption of

options.label: D
options.text: vitamin K in the large bowel

options.label: E
options.text: vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum

questions.why: Intrinsic factor binds dietary vitamin B12 after pancreatic enzymes release the vitamin from its earlier binding proteins. The complex is recognised by receptors in the terminal ileum, allowing absorption; intrinsic factor deficiency can therefore cause vitamin B12 deficiency.

notes.A: Iron is absorbed predominantly in the proximal small intestine through specialised iron transport mechanisms, rather than requiring intrinsic factor binding.
notes.B: Folate is absorbed mainly in the proximal small intestine through folate transport systems and does not depend on the intrinsic factor–cobalamin complex.
notes.C: Calcium absorption uses vitamin D-regulated and passive transport pathways, particularly in the small intestine, rather than depending on gastric intrinsic factor.
notes.D: Vitamin K absorption is associated mainly with intestinal lipid absorption and bile-dependent processes, rather than the terminal ileal intrinsic factor receptor pathway.

questions.stem: Gastrin, which stimulates acid secretion and gastric motility, is released by the

options.label: A
options.text: G cells of the gastric pits

questions.why: Gastrin comes from antral G cells and is triggered by vagal activity, luminal peptides and gastric distension.

questions.stem: During the gastric phase, distension of the stomach wall triggers acid secretion mainly through

options.label: C
options.text: release of secretin from the duodenum

questions.why: Gastric distension activates mechanosensitive pathways that initiate short enteric reflexes and long vagovagal reflexes. Excitatory neural signalling promotes acid secretion through direct parietal-cell stimulation and stimulation of gastrin and histamine pathways.

notes.A: Cholecystokinin is released mainly in response to duodenal nutrients and promotes pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction, rather than mediating the principal gastric stretch-induced acid response.
notes.C: Secretin is released in response to acidic duodenal chyme and chiefly stimulates bicarbonate secretion while opposing excessive gastric acid delivery.
notes.D: Circulating adrenaline participates in sympathetic stress responses but is not the principal mediator of the gastric distension-induced secretory reflexes.
notes.E: The enterogastric reflex is inhibitory feedback originating in the small intestine and generally limits gastric secretion and emptying rather than stimulating the gastric stretch response.

questions.stem: The intestinal phase ultimately inhibits gastric acid secretion through the

options.label: B
options.text: direct stretch of the gastric fundus

options.label: E
options.text: release of gastrin from antral G cells

questions.why: Acid, fat and other features of chyme entering the duodenum activate inhibitory neural feedback and release intestinal hormones, including secretin and cholecystokinin. Together with other enterogastrone signals, these responses limit gastric secretion and delivery of additional chyme.

notes.A: Histamine released from enterochromaffin-like cells stimulates parietal-cell H2 receptors and increases acid secretion, rather than providing the main intestinal inhibitory feedback.
notes.B: Gastric fundal stretch activates gastric-phase neural reflexes and receptive mechanisms, whereas intestinal-phase inhibition is initiated primarily by signals from the small intestine.
notes.D: Cephalic vagal reflexes prepare the stomach for food and generally stimulate gastric secretion before or during ingestion, rather than mediating duodenal inhibition.
notes.E: Antral gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion, so its release does not explain the principal inhibitory response to acidic or fatty duodenal contents.

questions.stem: Receptive relaxation of the proximal stomach as food arrives is mediated by

options.label: B
options.text: the proton pump of parietal cells

options.label: D
options.text: a vagovagal reflex with NANC transmitters

questions.why: Swallowing and gastric filling activate vagovagal reflexes that recruit inhibitory enteric motor neurons in the proximal stomach. Non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic signalling, particularly nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide, reduces muscle tone and accommodates food without a large pressure rise.

notes.A: Gastrin regulates gastric acid secretion and influences motor activity, but is not the principal inhibitory transmitter mediating receptive relaxation of proximal gastric smooth muscle.
notes.B: Parietal-cell proton pumps secrete hydrogen ions into gastric juice and do not directly mediate the neural relaxation of the proximal stomach.
notes.C: Pyloric contraction regulates distal gastric outflow and contributes to retropulsion, rather than directly producing receptive relaxation of the fundus and proximal body.
notes.E: Sympathetic effects can modify gastric motility, but receptive relaxation principally involves vagovagal activation of inhibitory enteric neurons in the proximal stomach.

questions.stem: The gastric 'pump' that grinds food and controls emptying is the
questions.why: The distal stomach, especially the antrum, generates strong phasic peristaltic contractions that propel food towards a regulated pyloric outlet. Retropulsion against the narrowed pylorus grinds and mixes solids, while coordinated antral and pyloric activity controls gastric emptying.

notes.A: The fundus and proximal body primarily provide accommodation and storage through receptive relaxation and tonic pressure, rather than producing the strongest grinding contractions.
notes.B: The cardia is the region near the gastro-oesophageal junction and is not the principal thick-walled grinding chamber that regulates delivery into the duodenum.
notes.C: The lower oesophageal sphincter controls entry from the oesophagus and limits reflux, rather than grinding food or controlling gastric outflow into the duodenum.
notes.D: The duodenum receives gastric chyme and supplies feedback regulating emptying, but the gastric grinding pump is located upstream in the distal stomach.

questions.stem: Gastric emptying is characteristically delayed by the presence in the duodenum of
questions.why: Acidic or fat-rich chyme in the duodenum activates enterogastric neural feedback and inhibitory hormonal signals, including secretin and cholecystokinin. These responses slow gastric delivery, allowing time for neutralisation, digestion and absorption in the small intestine.

notes.B: Dilute glucose solutions can evoke nutrient feedback, but excess duodenal acid and fat are especially characteristic potent inhibitors of gastric emptying.
notes.C: Water generally empties relatively rapidly because it requires little digestion and lacks the strong fat-related and acid-neutralisation feedback signals.
notes.D: Bicarbonate-rich chyme helps neutralise acid and does not provide the same acidic stimulus for inhibitory duodenal feedback as excess hydrogen ions.
notes.E: Protein digestion products can influence gastric emptying through intestinal feedback, but protein alone is not the exclusive or most characteristic inhibitory stimulus described here.

questions.stem: Trypsinogen is converted to active trypsin in the duodenum by
questions.why: Enteropeptidase, traditionally called enterokinase, is a duodenal brush-border enzyme that cleaves the activation peptide from trypsinogen to form trypsin. Active trypsin then activates additional trypsinogen and several other pancreatic digestive zymogens.

notes.A: Bile salts facilitate lipid emulsification and micelle formation, but they do not catalyse the specific proteolytic activation of pancreatic trypsinogen.
notes.C: Pepsin is an acid-active gastric protease that digests dietary protein, rather than the brush-border enzyme responsible for physiological trypsinogen activation.
notes.D: Gastric acid activates pepsinogen and denatures proteins, but pancreatic trypsinogen is normally activated enzymatically within the small intestinal lumen.
notes.E: Secretin stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion in response to duodenal acid and does not directly cleave trypsinogen into active trypsin.

questions.stem: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes chiefly to

options.label: A
options.text: let them be stored in the gallbladder

options.label: D
options.text: make them soluble in pancreatic juice

options.label: E
options.text: allow them to work at acidic pH

questions.why: Pancreatic proteases are synthesised and secreted as inactive zymogens to reduce premature digestion of pancreatic cells and ducts. Their physiological activation occurs predominantly in the small intestine, and pancreatic trypsin inhibitors provide an additional protective mechanism.

notes.A: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, whereas pancreatic digestive zymogens travel through the pancreatic duct system rather than being stored in the gallbladder.
notes.B: Bicarbonate neutralises gastric acid in the duodenum, but binding to bicarbonate is not the reason pancreatic proteases are secreted in inactive forms.
notes.D: Inactive zymogens can be transported in pancreatic juice, but their principal protective advantage is preventing inappropriate proteolytic activity within pancreatic tissue.
notes.E: Pancreatic proteases function mainly in the near-neutral or mildly alkaline small intestinal environment, rather than requiring inactive secretion to operate at gastric acidity.

questions.stem: Secretin, released from duodenal S cells by acidic chyme, mainly stimulates

options.label: E
options.text: enzyme secretion from pancreatic acinar cells

questions.why: Acid entering the duodenum stimulates S cells to release secretin into the circulation. Secretin activates pancreatic ductal signalling that promotes bicarbonate and water secretion, neutralising acidic chyme and providing an appropriate luminal pH for pancreatic enzymes.

notes.A: Gallbladder contraction is principally stimulated by cholecystokinin released in response to fats and protein digestion products, rather than being secretin's major action.
notes.B: Gastrin release is mainly regulated by gastric nutrients, distension and vagal signalling; secretin tends to inhibit excessive gastric acid secretion rather than stimulate gastrin.
notes.C: Parietal-cell acid secretion is stimulated by gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine, whereas secretin helps limit acid delivery and promotes its neutralisation.
notes.E: Pancreatic acinar enzyme secretion is principally stimulated by cholecystokinin and cholinergic input; secretin chiefly increases ductal bicarbonate-rich fluid secretion.

questions.stem: Cholecystokinin, released by duodenal I cells in response to peptides and fatty acids, stimulates

options.label: A
options.text: bicarbonate secretion from duct cells only

options.label: E
options.text: acinar enzyme output and gallbladder contraction

questions.why: Cholecystokinin is released from upper intestinal I cells in response to fatty acids and protein digestion products. It stimulates pancreatic digestive enzyme secretion through neural and hormonal pathways and promotes gallbladder contraction with coordinated biliary outflow.

notes.A: Secretin is the principal hormonal stimulus for pancreatic ductal bicarbonate secretion; cholecystokinin can potentiate this response but also strongly promotes enzyme secretion.
notes.B: Gastric acid secretion is principally stimulated by gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine; cholecystokinin more characteristically promotes intestinal digestive responses and slows gastric emptying.
notes.C: Salivary amylase release is regulated predominantly by autonomic neural stimulation of salivary glands, rather than by intestinal cholecystokinin as its main control signal.
notes.D: Intrinsic factor is secreted by gastric parietal cells to support vitamin B12 absorption, rather than being a principal target of cholecystokinin action.

questions.stem: Most of the pancreatic secretory response to a meal (50-80%) occurs during the
questions.why: The intestinal phase accounts for most meal-stimulated pancreatic secretion because acid and nutrients entering the duodenum trigger secretin and cholecystokinin release. These hormones and enteropancreatic neural reflexes promote ductal bicarbonate and acinar enzyme secretion.

notes.B: The cephalic phase uses vagal pathways activated by anticipation, sight and taste of food, but contributes less than the intestinal phase.
notes.C: Gastric distension stimulates vagovagal reflexes and some pancreatic secretion, but the strongest sustained pancreatic response follows entry of chyme into the duodenum.
notes.D: Interdigestive pancreatic secretion occurs during fasting in association with cyclic motor activity, rather than accounting for most meal-stimulated secretion.
notes.E: Oral sensory stimulation contributes to the cephalic response through neural pathways, but does not constitute the dominant phase of pancreatic secretion.

questions.stem: The liver cells that act as resident macrophages, recycling old red blood cells, are the
questions.why: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages associated with hepatic sinusoids, where they engulf microorganisms, cellular debris and damaged or aged erythrocytes. Their phagocytic activity contributes to iron recycling and clearance of material entering the liver from portal blood.

notes.A: Paneth cells reside at intestinal crypt bases and secrete antimicrobial substances, rather than acting as hepatic sinusoidal macrophages.
notes.C: Hepatocytes perform most hepatic metabolic, synthetic and secretory functions, while specialised macrophages provide much of the sinusoidal phagocytic activity.
notes.D: Hepatic stellate cells store vitamin A in the space of Disse and can produce fibrous matrix after injury, rather than serving as resident macrophages.
notes.E: Centroacinar cells form the initial portion of pancreatic intercalated ducts and contribute to ductal secretion, rather than performing hepatic erythrocyte clearance.

questions.stem: Hepatocytes receive a dual blood supply of oxygen-rich blood and nutrient-rich blood respectively from the

options.label: A
options.text: central vein and the cystic duct

options.label: B
options.text: splenic artery and the superior mesenteric vein

options.label: C
options.text: hepatic artery and the portal vein

options.label: D
options.text: portal vein and the hepatic artery

options.label: E
options.text: hepatic vein and the bile duct

questions.why: Hepatic arterial branches supply relatively oxygen-rich blood, while portal venous branches deliver nutrient-rich blood draining the digestive tract. Both streams enter hepatic sinusoids, where their mixture provides hepatocytes with substrates and oxygen before draining towards central veins.

notes.A: Central veins collect sinusoidal blood at lobular centres, while the cystic duct conducts bile to and from the gallbladder rather than supplying hepatocytes.
notes.B: The splenic artery supplies the spleen and adjacent organs, while the superior mesenteric vein contributes indirectly to hepatic portal inflow through the portal vein.
notes.D: The portal vein is the principal nutrient-rich inflow and the hepatic artery provides relatively oxygen-rich blood, so the proposed order reverses the requested sources.
notes.E: Hepatic veins drain blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava, whereas bile ducts carry bile rather than delivering a blood supply.

questions.stem: The two primary bile acids made by the liver are
questions.why: The human liver synthesises cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid from cholesterol. These are primary bile acids because they originate in hepatocytes, whereas intestinal bacterial metabolism produces secondary derivatives such as deoxycholic and lithocholic acids.

notes.A: Deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid are secondary bile acids produced by bacterial modification of cholic and chenodeoxycholic acids, respectively.
notes.B: Palmitic and stearic acids are saturated long-chain fatty acids, not the steroid-derived primary bile acids synthesised from cholesterol.
notes.C: Cholesterol is the precursor of bile acids and lecithin is a biliary phospholipid, but neither is itself one of the primary bile acids.
notes.E: Glycocholic and taurocholic acids are conjugated derivatives of cholic acid, rather than the two distinct unconjugated primary bile acids.

questions.stem: Bile acids are conjugated with which amino acids to form the more soluble bile salts?
questions.why: Hepatocytes conjugate bile acids with glycine or taurine through amide bond formation, reducing their pKa and increasing ionisation at intestinal pH. The resulting bile salts facilitate lipid emulsification and mixed micelle formation.

notes.A: Glutamine and alanine participate in nitrogen and carbon metabolism, but are not the normal conjugating substrates used to form human bile salts.
notes.B: Glycine is a normal bile acid conjugating substrate, whereas lysine is not the other physiological conjugating partner used by hepatocytes.
notes.C: Taurine participates in bile acid conjugation, but arginine is chiefly associated with pathways including the urea cycle and nitric oxide synthesis.
notes.D: Serine and cysteine contribute to several metabolic pathways, including taurine synthesis from cysteine, but neither is a standard direct bile acid conjugating substrate.

questions.stem: While stored in the gallbladder between meals, bile is concentrated roughly

options.label: A
options.text: five-fold by absorbing water and ions

options.label: B
options.text: ten-fold by secretion of bile acids

options.label: E
options.text: not at all, only stored unchanged

questions.why: During storage, gallbladder epithelium absorbs sodium chloride and other electrolytes, with water following osmotically. Most bile salts and other organic constituents remain in the lumen, allowing stored bile to become several times more concentrated, commonly around fivefold.

notes.B: Bile acids are secreted principally by hepatocytes, whereas gallbladder concentration results mainly from removal of water and electrolytes rather than additional bile acid secretion.
notes.C: Adding bicarbonate would not account for the usual concentration mechanism, which involves net absorption of electrolytes and water from stored bile.
notes.D: Active removal of bile salts from the gallbladder lumen would reduce the retained solute load rather than explaining concentration through water absorption.
notes.E: The gallbladder modifies stored bile substantially through epithelial fluid and electrolyte transport, so its role is not limited to passive storage.

questions.stem: Cholecystokinin promotes bile delivery to the duodenum by

options.label: B
options.text: contracting the gallbladder and relaxing the sphincter of Oddi

options.label: C
options.text: relaxing the gallbladder and contracting the sphincter of Oddi

questions.why: Cholecystokinin released after fat and protein enter the small intestine promotes contraction of gallbladder smooth muscle and coordinated relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. This raises gallbladder pressure while reducing outlet resistance, facilitating bile delivery into the duodenum.

notes.A: Closing the common bile duct would obstruct bile transport and increase upstream pressure rather than promoting delivery of stored bile to the intestine.
notes.C: Gallbladder relaxation with sphincter contraction favours retention of bile, opposing the coordinated emptying response normally stimulated by cholecystokinin after a meal.
notes.D: Secretin chiefly stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion from biliary duct epithelial cells, whereas cholecystokinin principally promotes the mechanical emptying of stored gallbladder bile.
notes.E: Hepatic bile acid synthesis is regulated strongly by enterohepatic feedback pathways; increasing synthesis is not the immediate mechanism of cholecystokinin-induced gallbladder emptying.

questions.stem: Pre-hepatic (haemolytic) jaundice is characterised by a rise in

options.label: C
options.text: unconjugated bilirubin from excessive red-cell breakdown

questions.why: Excessive erythrocyte breakdown increases haem degradation and bilirubin production before hepatic processing. When bilirubin delivery exceeds hepatic clearance capacity, circulating unconjugated bilirubin rises, producing the characteristic predominantly indirect hyperbilirubinaemia of haemolytic jaundice.

notes.A: Urinary urobilinogen can increase during haemolysis because more bilirubin reaches the intestine, but established haemolytic jaundice also involves increased circulating bilirubin.
notes.B: Bile acid concentrations can change with hepatobiliary disease, but isolated bile acid elevation does not explain the pigment accumulation caused by excessive erythrocyte breakdown.
notes.D: Biliary obstruction impairs excretion of conjugated bilirubin and typically produces predominantly direct hyperbilirubinaemia, rather than the characteristic pre-hepatic bilirubin pattern.
notes.E: Hepatocellular injury can impair bilirubin handling and produce mixed hyperbilirubinaemia, whereas haemolysis initially increases the unconjugated bilirubin load delivered to the liver.

questions.stem: Clinically visible jaundice typically appears once serum bilirubin exceeds about
questions.why: Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when bilirubin accumulates sufficiently in tissues, typically at serum concentrations around 2.5–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus may be recognised first, although visibility depends on lighting, examination and individual factors.

notes.A: Bilirubin concentrations of 10–12 mg/dL generally produce readily visible jaundice and are substantially above the usual clinical detection threshold.
notes.B: A bilirubin concentration near 1 mg/dL falls within or near the normal adult reference range and ordinarily does not produce visible jaundice.
notes.C: A serum bilirubin of 20 mg/dL represents marked hyperbilirubinaemia, rather than the approximate concentration at which clinical jaundice first becomes apparent.
notes.E: A concentration of 0.5 mg/dL is ordinarily within the normal adult range and is insufficient to produce visible bilirubin deposition.

questions.stem: Pigment gallstones form in the gallbladder largely because bilirubin, which is not absorbed there, becomes concentrated and precipitates as
questions.why: Pigment gallstones contain calcium bilirubinate, formed when poorly soluble unconjugated bilirubin combines with calcium in bile. Increased bilirubin load, deconjugation of bilirubin and biliary stasis can promote precipitation; gallbladder concentration alone does not explain every pigment stone.

notes.A: Cholesterol monohydrate crystallisation produces cholesterol-rich gallstones, whereas calcium bilirubinate precipitation characterises the pigment component of gallstones.
notes.B: Calcium oxalate is a common component of urinary calculi, rather than the principal bilirubin-derived material found in pigment gallstones.
notes.C: Uric acid crystals occur in conditions such as gout and certain urinary stones, but are not the precipitated bilirubin salt characteristic of pigment gallstones.
notes.D: Calcium phosphate can occur in mineral deposits and some stones, but the characteristic bilirubin-derived pigment is formed by calcium binding to bilirubinate.

questions.stem: Glucose and galactose are absorbed across the enterocyte brush border by
questions.why: Apical sodium–glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1) uses the sodium electrochemical gradient to drive glucose and galactose uptake into enterocytes. Basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase maintains that gradient, while monosaccharides usually leave towards blood through GLUT2.

notes.B: GLUT5 primarily transports fructose by facilitated diffusion across the intestinal brush border rather than performing sodium-coupled glucose and galactose uptake.
notes.C: GLUT2 normally mediates facilitated monosaccharide exit at the basolateral membrane; the classical apical sodium-dependent glucose and galactose entry pathway uses SGLT1.
notes.D: Glucose and galactose are hydrophilic molecules that do not cross lipid membranes efficiently by simple diffusion and therefore require specific transport proteins.
notes.E: Receptor-mediated endocytosis internalises selected macromolecules or ligand complexes, whereas glucose and galactose enter through membrane transporters rather than vesicular uptake.

questions.stem: Fructose crosses the brush border membrane by
questions.why: Apical GLUT5 mediates fructose uptake through facilitated diffusion down its concentration gradient, without directly coupling transport to sodium or ATP hydrolysis. Fructose subsequently leaves the enterocyte towards portal blood mainly through basolateral GLUT2.

notes.A: Fructose is a polar monosaccharide and crosses the brush-border membrane principally through a carrier, rather than through unrestricted simple lipid diffusion.
notes.C: SGLT1 couples sodium movement to glucose and galactose uptake, but it does not serve as the principal intestinal fructose transporter.
notes.D: GLUT2 mediates facilitated diffusion rather than active transport and is classically associated with basolateral monosaccharide exit from enterocytes.
notes.E: Proton-coupled carriers such as PEPT1 transport small peptides; dietary fructose instead uses a sodium-independent facilitative hexose transporter.

questions.stem: Salivary amylase contributes little to overall starch digestion because it is

options.label: E
options.text: unable to act on cooked starch

questions.why: Salivary amylase begins starch breakdown but is inactivated by gastric acid; pancreatic amylase completes it in the duodenum.

questions.stem: Lactose is split into glucose and galactose by the brush-border enzyme
questions.why: Lactase is an enzyme located at the small-intestinal brush border that hydrolyses the beta-1,4 glycosidic bond of lactose, releasing glucose and galactose. Reduced lactase activity leaves lactose available for osmotic water retention and bacterial fermentation.

notes.A: Maltase hydrolyses maltose and related alpha-linked glucose substrates, rather than cleaving the beta-linked glucose–galactose disaccharide lactose.
notes.B: Alpha-dextrinase, associated with isomaltase activity, hydrolyses alpha-1,6 branch linkages in starch digestion products rather than the linkage in lactose.
notes.C: Pancreatic amylase hydrolyses internal alpha-1,4 bonds in starch, but cannot cleave the beta-1,4 linkage connecting glucose and galactose in lactose.
notes.E: Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose, whereas lactose requires the distinct brush-border enzyme lactase to release galactose.

questions.stem: Protein digestion begins in the stomach with pepsin, which works optimally at a pH of about
questions.why: Pepsin is an acid-active gastric endopeptidase generated from pepsinogen in the acidic gastric lumen. Its activity is greatest at approximately pH 1.5–2.5, allowing initial protein digestion before pancreatic proteases take over in the small intestine.

notes.A: A pH of 6.5–7.0 is near neutral and better suits many intestinal enzymes; gastric pepsin has little activity under these conditions.
notes.B: A pH of 5.0–6.0 is less acidic than the optimum for pepsin, so its proteolytic activity is considerably reduced.
notes.C: A pH of 8.0–9.0 is alkaline and favours several pancreatic digestive enzymes rather than the acid-dependent gastric protease pepsin.
notes.D: A pH of 4.0–4.5 may permit some pepsin activity, but it lies above the usual optimal strongly acidic range.

questions.stem: Di- and tripeptides are absorbed across the brush border faster than free amino acids by a transporter coupled to

options.label: C
options.text: ATP hydrolysis at the apical membrane

questions.why: The brush-border transporter PEPT1 couples uptake of dipeptides and tripeptides to an inward hydrogen ion gradient. This gradient is supported indirectly by sodium–hydrogen exchange and basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase, while intracellular peptidases hydrolyse most absorbed peptides.

notes.B: Many free amino acid transporters use sodium gradients directly, but PEPT1 couples small peptide entry directly to hydrogen ions.
notes.C: The apical peptide transporter does not hydrolyse ATP itself; it uses a pre-existing proton electrochemical gradient as a secondary active transport mechanism.
notes.D: Chloride gradients support several epithelial electrolyte transport pathways but do not directly drive the principal brush-border uptake of dipeptides and tripeptides.
notes.E: Facilitated diffusion uses an existing substrate gradient without ion coupling, whereas PEPT1 uses proton cotransport to support peptide accumulation.

questions.stem: Dietary lipids are made accessible to water-soluble lipases in the duodenum by
questions.why: Amphipathic bile salts help stabilise small fat droplets formed during intestinal mixing, preventing their coalescence and increasing the lipid–water interface available to pancreatic lipase. They also form mixed micelles with products of lipid digestion.

notes.A: Intrinsic factor binds vitamin B12 for receptor-mediated ileal absorption and does not function as a detergent at the lipid–water interface.
notes.C: Dietary triglycerides are hydrolysed mainly to fatty acids and monoacylglycerols, rather than being converted into water-soluble sugars to permit digestion.
notes.D: Salivary amylase digests starch by cleaving alpha-linked glucose chains and does not emulsify triglycerides or perform their hydrolysis.
notes.E: Calcium soaps arise when fatty acids associate with calcium and may reduce absorption, rather than increasing lipid surface area for effective lipase action.

questions.stem: Pancreatic lipase requires which cofactor protein to act on emulsified fat droplets?
questions.why: Colipase binds pancreatic lipase and the lipid–water interface, helping lipase remain attached to bile salt-coated droplets. It enables efficient triglyceride hydrolysis despite the tendency of bile salts to interfere with lipase binding to the interface.

notes.A: Calmodulin is an intracellular calcium-binding regulatory protein involved in signalling, rather than an extracellular cofactor anchoring pancreatic lipase to dietary fat.
notes.B: Transferrin transports ferric iron in plasma and does not participate in the interaction between pancreatic lipase and emulsified lipid droplets.
notes.D: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen at the intestinal brush border; trypsin can activate procolipase, but enteropeptidase itself is not the required lipase-binding cofactor.
notes.E: Intrinsic factor supports vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum and has no principal role in anchoring pancreatic lipase to lipid droplets.

questions.stem: After re-esterification in the enterocyte, dietary lipids are packaged as chylomicrons that leave the cell and enter the
questions.why: Enterocytes re-esterify absorbed long-chain fatty acids and monoacylglycerols into triglycerides and package them with apolipoprotein B-48 into chylomicrons. These large particles enter intestinal lacteals and reach systemic venous blood through the lymphatic ducts.

notes.A: Shorter-chain fatty acids can enter portal blood more directly, but newly assembled chylomicrons predominantly follow the intestinal lymphatic route.
notes.B: Bile canaliculi carry bile between adjacent hepatocytes and are not channels through which intestinal enterocytes export newly assembled chylomicrons.
notes.C: The intestinal lumen is the site of lipid digestion and micelle delivery, whereas chylomicrons are normally exported from the basolateral side of enterocytes.
notes.E: Most newly formed chylomicrons are too large to readily enter ordinary mucosal blood capillaries and therefore enter the more permissive initial lymphatics.

questions.stem: Lipid digestion products are ferried through the watery layer to the brush border within

options.label: E
options.text: micelles of bile salts and lipid

questions.why: Mixed micelles contain bile salts and poorly water-soluble digestion products, including long-chain fatty acids, monoacylglycerols and cholesterol. They carry these lipids across the unstirred aqueous layer to the brush border, where lipids leave the micelles for absorption.

notes.A: Chylomicrons are lipoprotein particles assembled inside enterocytes after lipid absorption, rather than luminal carriers delivering digestion products to the brush border.
notes.B: Very-low-density lipoproteins are secreted predominantly by the liver to transport endogenous triglyceride through blood, rather than serving as intestinal luminal lipid carriers.
notes.C: Casein is a milk protein that can form colloidal particles, but does not provide the normal bile-dependent delivery mechanism for intestinal lipid digestion products.
notes.D: Albumin transports non-esterified fatty acids in blood, whereas poorly soluble intestinal lipid digestion products are delivered to the absorptive surface in mixed micelles.

questions.stem: Most water absorption in the gut is driven by

options.label: B
options.text: active pumping of water by aquaporins

options.label: D
options.text: secretion of bile into the duodenum

options.label: E
options.text: a chloride gradient set up by CFTR

questions.why: Intestinal water absorption is primarily passive and follows osmotic gradients generated by net electrolyte and nutrient absorption. Sodium transport, supported by basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase, is particularly important in promoting movement of water across epithelial and paracellular pathways.

notes.B: Aquaporins provide passive water channels and do not hydrolyse ATP to pump water independently against its osmotic gradient.
notes.C: Hydrostatic pressure can influence fluid movement, but net intestinal water absorption normally depends chiefly on osmotic gradients generated by solute transport.
notes.D: Bile delivers digestive substances and water to the intestinal lumen, rather than providing the main driving force for subsequent transepithelial water absorption.
notes.E: Apical CFTR-mediated chloride secretion generally draws sodium and water towards the intestinal lumen, rather than explaining most net water absorption.

questions.stem: Oral rehydration therapy works because water absorption is enhanced by the coupled uptake of
questions.why: Oral rehydration solution exploits preserved sodium–glucose cotransport through apical SGLT1, promoting sodium and glucose absorption even during many secretory diarrhoeal illnesses. Water follows net solute absorption osmotically, helping replace fluid and electrolyte losses.

notes.A: GLUT5 transports fructose without directly coupling its uptake to sodium, so fructose absorption does not provide the specific sodium–glucose cotransport mechanism exploited by rehydration solutions.
notes.C: Potassium and chloride replacement can be important during diarrhoea, but their uptake is not the principal glucose-dependent mechanism driving oral rehydration.
notes.D: Calcium and phosphate are absorbed through mineral-specific pathways, rather than the sodium–glucose cotransport mechanism that enhances water absorption during oral rehydration.
notes.E: Bicarbonate and hydrogen ions participate in epithelial acid–base transport, but oral rehydration depends primarily on maintained coupled sodium and glucose entry.

questions.stem: Calcium is actively absorbed, mainly in the duodenum, by a transcellular route whose entry step and calbindin are dependent on

options.label: A
options.text: parathyroid hormone acting directly on the gut

questions.why: Calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, increases expression of proteins supporting transcellular calcium absorption, including apical TRPV6 channels and intracellular calbindin. This pathway is particularly important in the duodenum when calcium intake is limited.

notes.A: Parathyroid hormone stimulates renal calcitriol production, thereby increasing intestinal calcium absorption indirectly rather than acting as the principal direct regulator of intestinal calbindin expression.
notes.B: Vitamin C promotes non-haem iron absorption through reducing and solubilising iron, but is not the principal hormonal regulator of intestinal calcium transport proteins.
notes.D: Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of selected proteins, including clotting and bone-associated proteins, rather than directly inducing the major intestinal calcium absorption pathway.
notes.E: Intrinsic factor is a gastric glycoprotein needed for efficient terminal ileal vitamin B12 uptake, rather than regulating calcium transport across duodenal enterocytes.

questions.stem: Non-haem dietary iron must be reduced from Fe3+ to Fe2+ before uptake, and then crosses the brush border via
questions.why: Most absorbable non-haem iron enters duodenal enterocytes as ferrous iron. Ferric iron can be reduced at the brush border by ferrireductases and dietary reducing agents, after which divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) mediates apical uptake.

notes.A: Transferrin binds ferric iron in plasma and delivers it to tissues through transferrin receptors, rather than mediating direct apical dietary iron uptake.
notes.B: Hephaestin is a ferroxidase associated with basolateral iron export, oxidising ferrous iron for transferrin binding rather than carrying it through the brush border.
notes.C: SGLT1 couples sodium entry to glucose and galactose uptake and does not transport ferrous iron into enterocytes.
notes.E: Ferroportin exports iron through the basolateral membrane towards the circulation, rather than transporting dietary ferrous iron across the apical brush border.

questions.stem: Export of iron from the enterocyte into the blood across the basolateral membrane is mediated by
questions.why: Ferroportin is the principal cellular iron exporter and transfers ferrous iron across the basolateral membrane of enterocytes. Ferroxidases including hephaestin facilitate oxidation to ferric iron, enabling its binding to circulating transferrin for systemic transport.

notes.A: DMT1 mediates uptake of divalent iron at the intestinal brush border rather than its principal basolateral export into the circulation.
notes.B: Calbindin is an intracellular calcium-binding protein that supports vitamin D-dependent calcium transport, rather than mediating the export of absorbed iron.
notes.C: Intrinsic factor forms a complex with vitamin B12 for ileal uptake and does not transport iron across the enterocyte basolateral membrane.
notes.D: GLUT2 transports monosaccharides by facilitated diffusion and has no principal role in exporting ferrous iron from the intestinal epithelium.

questions.stem: The liver-derived hormone that blocks intestinal iron absorption and release from stores is
questions.why: Hepcidin is a peptide hormone produced predominantly by hepatocytes that binds the iron exporter ferroportin, promoting its internalisation and degradation. Increased hepcidin therefore reduces iron transfer from enterocytes and iron release from macrophages and other storage cells.

notes.B: Transferrin binds and transports ferric iron through plasma, rather than hormonally suppressing cellular iron export by regulating ferroportin.
notes.C: Ferritin stores iron in a relatively safe intracellular form and reflects iron reserves, but is not the principal circulating regulator of ferroportin degradation.
notes.D: Erythropoietin stimulates erythrocyte production and can indirectly suppress hepcidin through erythroid signalling, rather than directly blocking intestinal iron export.
notes.E: Hephaestin oxidises exported ferrous iron to facilitate transferrin loading and therefore supports iron transfer rather than functioning as the inhibitory liver-derived hormone.

questions.stem: Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum requires it first to bind
questions.why: Vitamin B12 binds intrinsic factor after pancreatic enzymes degrade its initial binding protein in the duodenum. The intrinsic factor–B12 complex binds specialised receptors on terminal ileal enterocytes, permitting efficient receptor-mediated uptake of the vitamin.

notes.A: Calbindin facilitates intracellular calcium handling during transcellular absorption and is unrelated to the receptor-mediated intestinal uptake pathway for vitamin B12.
notes.C: Transferrin transports ferric iron in blood, whereas vitamin B12 relies on gastric intrinsic factor for efficient receptor-mediated uptake in the terminal ileum.
notes.D: Bile salts facilitate absorption of dietary lipids and fat-soluble vitamins, but vitamin B12 is water-soluble and follows a distinct binding-protein pathway.
notes.E: R-protein, or haptocorrin, initially binds vitamin B12 in the upper gastrointestinal tract, but efficient terminal ileal uptake requires transfer to intrinsic factor.

questions.stem: The fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are absorbed

options.label: A
options.text: by simple diffusion in the stomach

options.label: C
options.text: along the pathway for fat, within micelles

options.label: E
options.text: only in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor

questions.why: Vitamins A, D, E and K are lipid-soluble and depend substantially on normal fat digestion and bile salt micelle formation for efficient intestinal absorption. After uptake, they are commonly incorporated into chylomicrons for lymphatic transport.

notes.A: The stomach is not the principal site of absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; efficient uptake occurs mainly in the small intestine alongside lipid digestion.
notes.B: Transferrin carries iron in plasma and is not the luminal binding protein responsible for delivery of fat-soluble vitamins to intestinal absorptive cells.
notes.D: Sodium-coupled transport is important for several water-soluble nutrients, whereas fat-soluble vitamin absorption generally follows intestinal lipid-handling mechanisms.
notes.E: Intrinsic factor-dependent terminal ileal absorption is characteristic of vitamin B12, rather than the shared absorption pathway of vitamins A, D, E and K.

questions.stem: The driving force for fluid secretion by intestinal crypt enterocytes is active movement of

options.label: D
options.text: chloride into the lumen via the CFTR channel

options.label: E
options.text: sodium out of the lumen via the Na+ pump

questions.why: Cl- enters the cell via the basolateral Na+-K+-2Cl- carrier and exits apically through CFTR, drawing Na+ and water into the lumen.

questions.stem: Brunner's glands of the duodenum chiefly secrete
questions.why: Brunner's glands are submucosal glands concentrated in the proximal duodenum. Their alkaline mucous secretion helps lubricate the mucosa and protect it against acidic gastric chyme, complementing pancreatic and biliary bicarbonate secretion.

notes.A: Most major digestive enzymes entering the duodenal lumen originate from pancreatic acinar cells, while Brunner's glands chiefly provide protective mucus.
notes.B: Bile salts are produced by the liver and delivered through the biliary tract; Brunner's glands do not synthesise these lipid-emulsifying detergents.
notes.C: Intrinsic factor is produced by gastric parietal cells and supports vitamin B12 absorption rather than providing the principal protective secretion of duodenal submucosal glands.
notes.D: Hydrochloric acid is secreted by gastric parietal cells, whereas the alkaline secretion of Brunner's glands helps protect the duodenum from incoming gastric acid.

questions.stem: The longitudinal muscle of the colon is reduced to three bands called the
questions.why: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle representing concentrated portions of the outer longitudinal muscular layer of the colon. Their arrangement contributes to the characteristic sacculation of the colonic wall into haustra.

notes.B: Haustra are sacculations or pouches of the colonic wall, not the three longitudinal smooth-muscle bands contributing to their formation.
notes.C: Epiploic appendages are fat-filled peritoneal projections attached to the colon and are anatomically distinct from its longitudinal muscular bands.
notes.D: Plicae circulares are mucosal and submucosal folds characteristic of the small intestine that increase absorptive surface area, rather than bands of colonic muscle.
notes.E: Rugae are folds of the gastric mucosa and submucosa that flatten with distension, rather than the longitudinal smooth-muscle arrangement of the colon.

questions.stem: Strong contractions that sweep colonic contents toward the rectum a few times a day are called
questions.why: Colonic mass movements are strong, long-distance propulsive contractions that move substantial amounts of colonic contents towards the rectum. They occur intermittently, often after meals through gastrocolic responses, rather than continuously mixing contents within individual haustra.

notes.A: Receptive relaxation allows the proximal stomach to accommodate ingested food and does not describe strong distal propulsion of colonic contents.
notes.C: Haustral contractions principally mix colonic contents and expose them to the absorptive mucosa, rather than producing the characteristic long-distance mass propulsion.
notes.D: Segmentation redistributes luminal contents through local mixing contractions, whereas colonic mass movements produce substantial net movement towards the rectum.
notes.E: The migrating motor complex is a cyclic fasting motor pattern mainly associated with the stomach and small intestine, rather than postprandial colonic mass propulsion.

questions.stem: Entry of food into the stomach increases colonic motility and mass movements through the
questions.why: Gastric distension and meal-related neural and hormonal signalling increase colonic motor activity through the gastrocolic response. This may stimulate powerful propagating contractions towards the rectum, helping explain an urge to defaecate after eating.

notes.A: The cough reflex is a protective respiratory response involving coordinated airway and respiratory muscle activity, rather than a meal-related increase in colonic propulsion.
notes.B: Myenteric circuits coordinate local gastrointestinal motor activity, but the stomach-to-colon response is specifically the gastrocolic reflex and involves broader regulatory signalling.
notes.D: The enterogastric reflex provides inhibitory feedback from the small intestine to the stomach, whereas the gastrocolic reflex increases colonic activity following gastric filling.
notes.E: The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex involves pulmonary stretch receptor feedback regulating inspiration, rather than communication between gastric filling and colonic motility.

questions.stem: The internal anal sphincter differs from the external one in that it is

options.label: A
options.text: skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve

options.label: C
options.text: controlled entirely by the sympathetic chain

questions.why: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of involuntary circular smooth muscle and is regulated by intrinsic myogenic, enteric and autonomic mechanisms. Rectal distension triggers its relaxation through the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, while the external sphincter provides voluntary skeletal-muscle control.

notes.A: Skeletal muscle supplied by the pudendal nerve characterises the external anal sphincter, rather than the involuntary internal smooth-muscle sphincter.
notes.B: Cardiac muscle is specialised striated muscle of the heart; the internal anal sphincter is formed by gastrointestinal circular smooth muscle.
notes.C: Sympathetic input can support internal sphincter tone, but intrinsic myogenic activity and enteric inhibitory pathways also regulate it, so control is not exclusively sympathetic.
notes.E: Voluntary skeletal-muscle control belongs principally to the external anal sphincter and pelvic floor, rather than the involuntary internal anal sphincter.

questions.stem: The defecation reflex is integrated in the
questions.why: Rectal distension activates an intrinsic enteric defaecation reflex and a stronger parasympathetic spinal reflex integrated at sacral segments S2–S4. Pelvic splanchnic pathways reinforce rectal contraction and coordinate evacuation, while supraspinal control helps regulate voluntary continence.

notes.A: Medullary emetic circuits coordinate vomiting and upper gastrointestinal expulsion, rather than the sacral parasympathetic component of rectal evacuation.
