notes.B: Thoracolumbar sympathetic pathways influence pelvic organ tone and continence, but the major parasympathetic defaecation reflex is integrated in the sacral spinal cord.
notes.C: The pontine micturition centre coordinates urinary bladder emptying and urethral sphincter activity, rather than the principal spinal defaecation reflex.
notes.D: Cortical control enables voluntary postponement or facilitation of defaecation, but reflex rectal motor responses also involve enteric and sacral spinal circuits.

questions.stem: The chemoreceptor trigger zone that can initiate vomiting lies in the

options.label: A
options.text: area postrema of the fourth ventricle

options.label: E
options.text: dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

questions.why: The chemoreceptor trigger zone is associated with the area postrema on the dorsal medulla near the floor of the fourth ventricle. Its relatively permeable blood–brain barrier allows detection of circulating emetic substances that activate brainstem vomiting networks.

notes.B: Pontine reticular circuits participate in several motor and autonomic functions, but the classic blood-borne emetic chemosensory region is the medullary area postrema.
notes.C: The nucleus tractus solitarius integrates visceral afferent and emetic signals, but the classical chemoreceptor trigger zone is located in the adjacent area postrema.
notes.D: Hypothalamic satiety circuits regulate feeding and energy homeostasis, rather than forming the specialised circumventricular chemosensory site associated with vomiting.
notes.E: The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus supplies parasympathetic output to visceral organs, rather than being the principal blood-borne emetic chemoreceptor trigger zone.

questions.stem: Urea, the main nitrogenous waste, is synthesised by the
questions.why: Hepatocytes convert potentially toxic ammonia into urea through the urea cycle, whose reactions occur in both mitochondria and cytosol. Urea enters blood and is eliminated principally by the kidneys, providing a major pathway for nitrogen disposal.

notes.A: The spleen filters blood and participates in erythrocyte clearance and immunity, rather than performing the principal complete urea cycle for nitrogen disposal.
notes.C: The kidneys filter and excrete urea and produce ammonium for acid–base regulation, but most circulating urea is synthesised in the liver.
notes.D: Intestinal mucosal cells participate in amino acid metabolism and supply nitrogen-containing metabolites, but do not account for the principal whole-body urea synthesis pathway.
notes.E: Pancreatic acinar cells synthesise and secrete digestive enzymes, rather than serving as the main site of ammonia detoxification through the urea cycle.

questions.stem: Plasma proteins such as albumin, prothrombin and fibrinogen are synthesised chiefly by the
questions.why: Hepatocytes synthesise albumin and many plasma coagulation proteins, including fibrinogen and prothrombin. Albumin contributes to plasma oncotic pressure and solute transport, while fibrinogen and prothrombin participate in haemostasis; hepatic dysfunction can therefore impair these functions.

notes.A: The spleen contributes to immune surveillance and clearance of blood cells, rather than synthesising most circulating albumin and hepatic coagulation proteins.
notes.B: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes and endocrine hormones, rather than supplying the principal circulating albumin, prothrombin and fibrinogen pool.
notes.D: The kidneys produce regulatory substances such as renin and erythropoietin, but most of the specified plasma proteins are synthesised by hepatocytes.
notes.E: Bone marrow produces blood cells and contains antibody-producing plasma cells, but the listed albumin and coagulation proteins are predominantly hepatic products.

questions.stem: The recycling of bile salts from the ileum back to the liver for re-secretion is known as the
questions.why: Enterohepatic circulation recycles bile salts secreted by the liver into the intestine, most of which are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum. Portal venous blood returns them to hepatocytes for uptake and resecretion, conserving the bile acid pool.

notes.A: Splanchnic circulation encompasses blood flow through abdominal digestive organs, but does not specifically name the repeated intestinal absorption and hepatic resecretion of bile salts.
notes.B: Lymphatic circulation transports lymph and absorbed chylomicrons towards systemic veins, whereas most reabsorbed bile salts return to the liver through portal blood.
notes.C: Countercurrent exchange describes transfer between closely associated flows moving in opposite directions, rather than the recycling loop linking intestinal absorption and biliary secretion.
notes.E: Portal circulation provides the venous return pathway for absorbed bile salts, but enterohepatic circulation specifically includes both that return and subsequent biliary resecretion.
